question: On International Rare Disease Day, 28 February 2025, we will demonstrate our solidarity with approximately 27 to 36 million people living with a rare disease in the EU. The inclusion of these individuals in our societies is vital, but despite commendable initiatives, such as the European Reference Networks, they still face health and social inequities.

Market and patient access to orphan medicinal products or treatments is a widely recognised issue of near-unpayability for individuals and Member States’ healthcare systems. Research into and development of orphan therapies must remain a priority of European pharmaceutical policy.
However, the increasing costs of orphan medicines on Member States’ healthcare budgets may challenge solidarity with rare disease patients. 1.
Does the Commission agree with the identified opportunities and gaps in research and knowledge, diagnosis and codification, market failure, market access, patient access and high prices?

Will the Commission propose an overarching action plan on rare diseases that addresses remaining opportunities and creates a European policy framework to support the revision of national plans for rare diseases?
Does the Commission intend to create a European financial solidarity instrument to improve access to rare disease treatments?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.6.2025)

Challenges around orphan drugs are manifold. Medical requirements of patients with rare diseases (RD) are not adequately met, affordability of products is a growing challenge for individuals and health systems, and the existing regulatory framework does not sufficiently cater for innovation.

The Commission has taken strong actions on RD notably with the European Reference Networks (ERN), making expertise travel and disseminate. To maximise the benefits already offered by the ERNs, their integration into national healthcare systems is needed. A Joint Action is underway until 2027 to achieve this goal1, providing a clearer picture of the RD landscape in the EU and informing future decisions.

The ongoing revision of pharmaceutical legislation2 promotes the development of treatments for RD via regulatory incentives and enhanced scientific support from the European Medicines Agency. It focuses on areas where patients have no treatment options3, facilitating faster access to innovative medicines and affordable medicines.

The Commission supports ORPHANET’s work on RD nomenclature and high-quality information on RD codification4. ERNs for RD5 have conducted over 4,000 virtual panels on RD patients since 2017. Collaborative research on RD has been a Commission priority6 since 2006, when it first coordinated research funding with national agencies7.

Recently it launched its fourth successor, the European Partnership ERDERA8, and at global level9. The Innovative Health Initiative also supports RD research10. Gaps are tackled from various angles: treatments11, diagnoses12, newborn screening13, Health Technology Assessment14, specific regulatory needs15, inclusion of RD patients, and through relevant projects16. 1 JARDIN Joint Action https://jardin-ern.eu/.

EU funding enables better treatment for RD patients. While a financial solidarity instrument is not currently in the pipeline, in 2023 the Commission funded via EU4Health the ERNs for another four years with EUR 77.4 million. Besides, Directive 2011/24/EU17 supports crossborder healthcare, including for RD. Its evaluation in 2027 will guide next steps.
